definition: Correlate means to vary together — when two things correlate, changes in one are matched by changes in the other across the record.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word correlate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know correlate should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Coincide is weaker than correlate: two schedules can coincide once, at a single shared moment, while correlating takes a whole record of rises and falls that keep answering each other.
Synchronize goes further than correlate — correlated things move together loosely, lag and all, while synchronized things are locked to the same beat, matched moment for moment.

Correspond says two things match up, point for point — a map corresponds to the terrain even though neither ever changes. Correlate adds movement: correlated things vary together, each shift in one answered by a shift in the other.

Correlate means to vary together — when two things correlate, changes in one are matched by changes in the other across the record.
Since the shop opened, the owner of Spoke & Chain has penciled two numbers into her day book every Friday: the week's average gas price and the number of bikes sold.
Laid side by side, the columns correlate — when gas climbs a dime, sales tick upward within a week or two, and the long flat stretches match almost line for line.
She has stopped guessing at spring inventory; she reads the fuel report instead, letting one column tell her where the other is headed.
Correlate is the exact word for those two columns, because correlate means to vary together — changes in one matched by changes in the other across the whole record.
Notice what the word does not claim: it never says expensive gas causes bike sales, only that the two move in step.
That restraint is the point.
A researcher who reports that two things correlate is describing a pattern and stopping there, one careful step short of naming a cause.
Correlate is the cautious verb of charts and studies: it reports that two things move together and claims nothing more.
Ascribe, its unit-mate, goes a step further — to ascribe is to assign a cause outright, which is exactly the step correlate refuses to take.
Correspond leans static, a point-for-point match; link is the loose everyday verb.
When a researcher is not yet ready to say 'because,' correlate is the word that holds the line.

When the city installed its bike-share stations, planners began logging two numbers side by side: daily riders and the downtown air-quality index.
Three years in, the pattern is hard to miss.
The two measures correlate: in months when ridership climbs, the pollution index slides, and when winter thins the riders out, the index creeps back up.
Skeptics first shrugged it off, pointing to one rainy spring when both numbers happened to fall together and calling the whole thing luck.
But the analysts kept charting, and the paired movement held across thirty-six months, in every season and in every district they measured.
The council now treats the two curves as a single instrument: nudge one, they say, and expect the other to answer within a quarter.
